faq: Do I need 10,000 steps?
No. 10,000 began as a marketing number. Studies link benefits to totals well below it, and the guideline is written in minutes, not steps: 150 or more a week at moderate effort.
Can I walk on a treadmill?
Yes. Set a 1% incline to roughly match outdoor effort.
What if 10 minutes is too much?
Start with 5 minutes twice a day and repeat week one until it feels comfortable.

title: 14-day sleep reset
summary: Two weeks of one small change a night to steady your body clock.
lead: Most sleep trouble that is not medical comes down to timing, light and wind-down. This reset changes one thing each day and keeps everything you have already added.
rules: Each day adds one habit. Keep the earlier ones going.
The single most important rule is the fixed wake-up time. Hold it at weekends too.
If you cannot sleep after about 20 minutes, get up, do something quiet in low light and return when sleepy.
Loud snoring with pauses, or weeks of poor sleep despite good habits, deserves a doctor's visit.
tasks: Choose your wake-up time. Set the alarm for it every day this fortnight.
Get outside for 10 minutes of daylight within an hour of waking.
Work out your caffeine cut-off time and stick to it.
Count back from your wake-up time to set a bedtime that allows 7 to 9 hours.
Dim the lights and screens for the last hour of the evening.
Charge your phone outside the bedroom.
Make the room darker: cover LEDs, close the gaps in the curtains.
Cool the bedroom to around 18°C (65°F), or open a window.
Build a 20-minute wind-down in the same order every night.
Finish alcohol at least 3 hours before bed, or skip it.
Finish your last big meal 3 hours before bed.
Move your body today, but finish hard exercise 3 hours before bed.
Write tomorrow's to-do list before your wind-down, then close the notebook.
Review: which three changes helped most? Those are your keepers.
faq: I work shifts. Can I do this?
Yes, but anchor to your main sleep period rather than the clock: light on waking, dark and cool for sleep, a steady routine on each run of shifts.
Should I use a sleep tracker?
Optional. How rested you feel during the day is the better measure. If tracking makes you anxious about sleep, leave it off.
keywords: sleep reset, fix sleep schedule, sleep challenge

title: 7-day sugar-smart challenge
summary: A week of finding and trimming added sugar, one easy swap a day.
lead: This is not a no-sugar week. It is seven days of noticing where added sugar comes from in your own diet and making one swap at a time. Fruit, plain milk and plain yoghurt are not the target.
rules: Added sugar is what is put in during processing or at the table. Whole fruit does not count.
One swap a day. Keep the ones that were painless.
Read the 'added sugars' or 'of which sugars' line on labels.
Not suitable as a weight-loss diet. If you have diabetes, keep following your care plan.
tasks: List everything sweet you drink in a day. Drinks are the biggest single source for most people.
Swap one sugary drink for water, sparkling water or unsweetened tea.
Read the label on your breakfast cereal, yoghurt or bread. Find one with less added sugar.
Check your sauces: ketchup, pasta sauce and dressings. Pick one lower-sugar option.
Have fruit, nuts or plain yoghurt in place of one sweet snack.
Halve the sugar or syrup in your tea, coffee or porridge.
Decide which three swaps you will keep. Write them down.
faq: How much added sugar is too much?

The WHO advises keeping free sugars under 10% of daily energy, and says under 5% (about 25 g or 6 teaspoons) brings extra benefit. The 2025–2030 U.S. guidelines say no amount is needed in a healthy diet.
Are sweeteners better?
They cut calories, but evidence on long-term benefit is mixed, and the WHO advises against relying on them for weight control. Water and unsweetened drinks are the simplest choice.

lead: Week one attaches water to things you already do. Week two makes it easier to reach. Week three hits your full target every day. Work out your target first with the water intake calculator.
rules: Find your target with the water intake calculator before you begin.
All unsweetened drinks count. Tea and coffee count too.
Spread drinks through the day rather than catching up at night.
If you have been told to limit fluids for a heart or kidney condition, follow that advice instead.

Add a slice of lemon, cucumber or mint to keep it interesting.
Drink a glass before and after any exercise.
Swap a second sweet drink for sparkling water or unsweetened tea.
Check the colour: pale yellow means you are on track.
Hit your full daily target once this week. Today is a good day.
Full target today. Tick it off before dinner.
Full target, with most of it before 6 pm so sleep is not disturbed.
Full target. Notice your energy mid-afternoon.
Full target. Eat two water-rich foods: fruit, soup, salad or yoghurt.

faq: Is eight glasses a day the rule?
It is a fair rough guide but not a requirement. Needs vary with body size, activity and heat. Thirst and pale-yellow urine are reliable signals for most healthy adults.
Can I drink too much?
Yes, though it is rare. Drinking several litres in a short time can dilute blood sodium. Spread your intake and do not force it far beyond thirst.

title: 10-day calm challenge
summary: Ten short daily practices that take the edge off stress, none longer than ten minutes.
lead: Stress is not the enemy; having no way to come down from it is. Each day you try one small, well-studied practice. By day ten you will know which two or three work for you.
rules: Each practice takes 2 to 10 minutes.
Do it at the same time each day if you can; after lunch works well.
You are testing what suits you. Not every practice will.
If low mood or anxiety is getting in the way of daily life, or you feel unsafe, talk to a doctor or a local helpline. This challenge is not treatment.
tasks: Two minutes of slow breathing: in for 4, out for 6.
A 10-minute walk outdoors without headphones. Notice five things you can see.
Write down what is on your mind for 5 minutes, then close the notebook.
Box breathing for 3 minutes: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4.
Tense and release each muscle group from feet to face, 5 minutes.
One phone-free hour this evening.
Write three specific things that went well today.
Do one task with full attention: tea, a shower, washing up.
Tell someone one thing you appreciate about them.
Choose your two favourite practices and schedule them for next week.
faq: Does breathing really change stress?
Slow breathing with a longer out-breath nudges the nervous system towards its rest state and lowers heart rate. Trials show small to moderate reductions in self-reported stress and anxiety.
I can't sit still to meditate. Is that a problem?
No. Walking, stretching and focused chores count. The skill is returning your attention, not sitting motionless.

title: 7-day reach-out challenge
summary: One small act of connection a day for a week.
lead: Strong relationships are linked with longer, healthier lives, and they are built from small, repeated contact. Each task here takes minutes.
rules: Keep it small. A two-line message counts.
Aim for real exchanges, not likes or reactions.
If someone does not reply, that is about their week, not about you.
Feeling persistently lonely is common and nothing to be ashamed of. A doctor or community organisation can point you to local groups.
tasks: Message someone you have not spoken to in months. Say what made you think of them.
Have one conversation today with no phone in your hand.
Thank someone and say exactly what for.
Ask a neighbour, colleague or shop assistant a real question, and listen.
Call a relative or old friend for ten minutes.
Invite someone to do something this week: a walk, a coffee, a meal.
Put one recurring catch-up in your calendar.
faq: I'm an introvert. Do I need lots of friends?
No. The research points to the quality and reliability of a few relationships, not the number.
Does online contact count?
A video call or a long message thread with someone you know counts. Passive scrolling does not have the same effect.
keywords: social connection challenge, loneliness, reach out

title: Know-your-numbers week
summary: Seven days, seven measurements. Finish with a one-page picture of your health basics.
lead: Most people do not know their blood pressure, waist measurement or resting heart rate. This week you collect one number a day, using a tape measure, a clock and the free tools on this site.
rules: One number a day. Each takes under ten minutes.
Everything is saved to My numbers in this browser.
Numbers are for awareness. Only a health professional can diagnose.
A blood pressure reading above 180/120, especially with symptoms, needs urgent medical attention.
tasks: Measure your height and weight and note your BMI.
Measure your waist and work out your waist-to-height ratio.
Take your resting heart rate first thing in the morning.
Get a blood pressure reading at home or at a pharmacy.
Add up your active minutes for the past week.
Count your alcoholic drinks and your caffeine for a typical week.
Check which screenings are due at your age, and book anything overdue.
faq: I don't have a blood pressure monitor.
Many pharmacies offer free checks, and a validated upper-arm home monitor is inexpensive. Sit quietly for five minutes first.
What do I do with the numbers?
Open My numbers to see them together, and take the list to your next checkup. Trends over time matter more than any single reading.
